lead: A multi-speed gearbox turns one input speed into a set of stepped output speeds. It places gear groups in series, and the number of speeds is the product of the number of ratios in each group. A lathe, drilling machine or milling machine needs these steps because the best spindle speed changes with the job diameter and the material. The speeds follow a geometric progression, and a ray diagram, drawn on a log scale, shows every ratio and every speed of the design at a glance, so the designer can check it before fixing tooth numbers.
prereq: You need: speed ratios of gear pairs and compound trains from gear trains.

blocks.text: Let the spindle have z speeds from nmin to nmax. The speed range is a ratio, Rn = nmax/nmin. Spaced geometrically, each speed is the one below it times the step ratio φ (progression ratio):
φ = (nmax/nmin)1/(z − 1) There are z − 1 steps between z speeds; φ has no unit. Then n2 = n1φ, n3 = n1φ², and so on.

Geometric steps give the same percentage change everywhere. With arithmetic steps of 50 rpm, going from 100 to 150 rpm is a 50 % jump but 500 to 550 rpm only 10 %, so the machine would be coarse at low speeds and needlessly fine at high speeds. The cutting speed v = πDn/1000 (m/min, D in mm) is what the job needs, and a geometric series loses the same fraction of it at every step.

Standard step ratios come from the preferred number series: 1.06, 1.12, 1.26, 1.41, 1.58 and 2.0 (R40, R20, R10, R20/3, R5 and R10/3 series); 1.26 and 1.41 are the most common in machine tools. The standard speeds are the rounded series values, for example 100, 140, 200, 280, 400, 560 rpm for φ = 1.41. If the calculated φ falls between two standard values, take the nearer one and adjust n<sub>max</sub>.

The structure formula writes the number of speeds as a product, z = p1 × p2 × …, where p1 is the number of ratios in the first group (nearest the motor), p2 in the second, and so on. Each group also has a characteristic x, the number of steps of φ between neighbouring ratios of that group, written in brackets: 6 = 3(1) 2(3) means a first group of three ratios one step apart and a second group of two ratios three steps apart. The first group with x = 1 is the basic group; the next has x equal to the number of speeds produced before it.

A ray diagram (speed chart) draws one vertical line per shaft and one horizontal line per standard speed, spaced equally because the scale is logarithmic in φ. A gear pair is a ray from its input speed on one shaft to its output speed on the next. A horizontal ray is a 1:1 pair; a ray falling by j speed lines has the ratio 1/φj. Rays of one group from one point fan out, with neighbouring rays x speed lines apart; rays of the same pair drawn from different points are parallel, because they are the same ratio.

Rules that keep the gears sensible: in any group the reduction should be no more than 1/4 and the step-up no more than 2 (so a group's ratios span at most 8); keep each shaft as fast as possible for as long as possible, so put the big reductions in the last group, where the torque is largest anyway; and give the groups near the motor the most ratios (p<sub>1</sub> ≥ p<sub>2</sub> ≥ …) so that the slower, heavier shafts carry fewer gears. The diagram must give every output speed once, with no two rays landing on the same speed.

sections.h3: From the ray diagram to the gearbox

blocks.text: Within one group all pairs share the same two shafts, so they must have the same centre distance: with one module, z<sub>driver</sub> + z<sub>driven</sub> is the same for every pair of the group. The tooth numbers come from the ratios and a chosen sum, with no gear below about 17 teeth. The actual speeds may differ a little from the standard ones; a deviation within ±10(φ − 1) % is accepted, ±4.1 % for φ = 1.41.

The gearing (kinematic) diagram is the side view of the same design: shafts, the gears on each, and which pairs mesh for each speed. Speeds are selected by sliding gear clusters on splined shafts, cheap but shifted only when stopped, by dog clutches, or by friction clutches that can shift under load. A Norton gearbox, used for feed and thread-cutting drives, has a cone of gears on one shaft and a swinging tumbler gear that meshes with any one of them, giving many ratios in a small space. A car gearbox uses the same idea with a few widely spaced ratios.

spec.aria: Ray diagram with three shafts and six speed lines from 100 to 560 revolutions per minute; three rays from shaft I, then two rays from each speed on shaft II.

examples.question: A six-speed spindle has n<sub>min</sub> = 100 rpm and φ = 1.41. Find all six speeds, the maximum speed and the speed range.
steps: Rounded to the standard series: 100, 140, 200, 280, 400, 560 rpm.
Range: R<sub>n</sub> = 557.3/100 = 5.57 (5.6 with the standard speeds), which is φ⁵.

examples.question: Design the gearbox for these six standard speeds with the structure 6 = 3(1) 2(3). Shaft I runs at 560 rpm. Draw the ray diagram, find the tooth numbers of each pair with one module and check the output speeds.
steps: Group a (shaft I to II), three ratios one step apart: 1, 1/1.41, 1/2, giving 560, 400 and 280 rpm on shaft II. The largest reduction 1/2 is inside the 1/4 limit.
Group b (shaft II to III), two ratios three steps apart: 1 and 1/φ³ = 1/2.8. From 560, 400 and 280 rpm they give 560, 400, 280 and 200, 140, 100 rpm on shaft III: all six speeds, none twice.
Teeth of group a with a sum of 72: 1:1 gives 36/36; 1:1.41 gives 72/2.41 = 29.9, so 30/42; 1:2 gives 24/48.
Teeth of group b with a sum of 76: 1:1 gives 38/38; 1:2.8 gives 76/3.8 = 20, so 20/56. Smallest gear 20 teeth, above the undercut limit.
Actual speeds: 560 × 30/42 = 400; 560 × 24/48 = 280; then × 20/56: 200.0, 142.9 and 100.0 rpm. Only 142.9 differs from the standard 140, by 2.0 %, inside the allowed 4.1 %.

traps: Using an arithmetic progression because the numbers look neat; spindle speeds are geometric.
Taking the speed range as n<sub>max</sub> − n<sub>min</sub> instead of n<sub>max</sub>/n<sub>min</sub>, or dividing by z instead of z − 1 in the step-ratio formula.
Accepting a ray diagram in which two rays land on the same speed: that design gives fewer than z distinct speeds.
Breaking the group limits: a reduction beyond 1/4 or a step-up beyond 2 in one pair makes one gear too large.
Forgetting that every pair in a group has the same centre distance, so the tooth sums must be equal (for one module).

quiz.q: Define the speed range and the step ratio of a z-speed gearbox.
What does the structure formula 12 = 3(1) 2(3) 2(6) mean?
quiz.a: Three groups: three ratios one step apart, then two ratios three steps apart, then two ratios six steps apart, giving 12 speeds.

quiz.q: Why are spindle speeds spaced geometrically?
quiz.a: Geometric steps change the speed by the same percentage everywhere, so the loss of cutting speed between steps is the same at low and high speeds.

quiz.q: Why are the large reductions put in the last group?
quiz.a: The shafts before it then run fast and carry small torques, so their shafts and gears stay small; only the last shaft carries the large torque.

quiz.q: A 9-speed gearbox has n<sub>min</sub> = 40 rpm and n<sub>max</sub> = 1000 rpm. Find φ and the nearest standard value.
quiz.a: R<sub>n</sub> = 25; φ = 25<sup>1/8</sup> = 1.495; the nearest standard value is 1.58 (or 1.41 with n<sub>max</sub> adjusted).

quiz.q: A 6-speed gearbox has n<sub>min</sub> = 200 rpm and φ = 1.25. Find n<sub>6</sub>.
In a ray diagram, two rays of the last group land on the same speed line. What does it mean and how is it fixed?
quiz.a: Two gear paths give the same output speed, so the box has fewer distinct speeds than planned. Change the characteristic of that group (for example from 2 to 3) so its rays are spread by the number of speeds produced before it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most CNC machine tools now use a variable-speed spindle motor with a two- or three-step gearbox for torque, so long stepped gearboxes survive mainly in conventional and heavy machines. Automatic car transmissions reach eight to ten ratios with planetary sets and clutches instead of sliding gears. Search for ray diagram design of machine tool gearboxes, preferred numbers (ISO 3) and spindle drive design.
